# RdistNN

<!-- badges: start -->
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/JakobJuergens/RdistNN/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/JakobJuergens/RdistNN/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![test-coverage](https://github.com/JakobJuergens/RdistNN/actions/workflows/test-coverage.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/JakobJuergens/RdistNN/actions/workflows/test-coverage.yaml)
<!-- badges: end -->

**RdistNN** estimates conditional treatment effects and regression functions
using distributional nearest-neighbor (DNN) weights. Fit at selected covariate
profiles, report pointwise estimates and delete-one jackknife standard errors,
and inspect localization, overlap and sensitivity to tuning choices.

CATE and nonparametric regression are the main workflows. The development
version also provides **experimental conditional LATE (CLATE)** estimation
with the same reporting and plotting interfaces. You supply nuisance
predictions for the causal estimators; RdistNN constructs the adjusted signals
and performs the local estimation and inference calculations.

[Get started](https://JakobJuergens.github.io/RdistNN/articles/getting-started.html)
· [Function reference](https://JakobJuergens.github.io/RdistNN/reference/index.html)
· [CLATE guide](https://JakobJuergens.github.io/RdistNN/articles/conditional-late.html)
· [Report an issue](https://github.com/JakobJuergens/RdistNN/issues)

## Installation

Install the **development version** from GitHub to use all functionality
shown below, including CLATE and its shared plotting and tuning interfaces:

```r
install.packages("pak")  # once
pak::pak("JakobJuergens/RdistNN")
```

R 4.1.0 or newer, Rcpp and a C++17 toolchain are required. Use Rtools matching
your R version on Windows, Xcode command line tools on macOS, or an R-compatible
C++ compiler on Linux. OpenMP is optional; supported kernels run serially when
it is unavailable. Install `ggplot2` for plots and `patchwork` for composed
dashboards:

```r
install.packages(c("ggplot2", "patchwork"))  # optional
```

For the **tagged release**, use `pak::pak("JakobJuergens/RdistNN@v0.1.0")`.
[Release 0.1.0](https://github.com/JakobJuergens/RdistNN/releases/tag/v0.1.0)
contains the original CATE and regression workflows; it does **not** include
the recent CLATE functionality. Its release assets include a source package
with built HTML vignettes and checksums. The online documentation describes
the development version.

## Choose a workflow

| Goal | Entry point | Inputs and scope |
|---|---|---|
| Conditional average treatment effects | `cate_dnn()` | Outcome, binary treatment and supplied outcome/propensity predictions, or a supplied pseudo-outcome |
| Conditional mean regression | `np_dnn()` | Outcome and covariates; no nuisance predictions needed |
| Conditional effects among compliers | `clate_dnn()` | Binary instrument and treatment, outcome, and five supplied nuisance predictions; **experimental** |
| A ratio of two local conditional means | `affine_ratio_dnn()` | Two aligned signals, with paired covariance; **experimental** |
| Two-scale regression | `np_tdnn()` | Signed combination of two DNN scales; additional smoothness conditions |

The estimators accept numeric matrices/vectors or a data frame (including a
tibble) with explicit column selectors. Use `x0` for one reporting profile or
`X0` for a matrix of profiles. CATE and CLATE support single-scale
`method = "exact"` (default) and `method = "asymp"` DNN weights. Two-scale
TDNN is available for nonparametric regression only.

## Conditional average treatment effects

This example uses simulated data and **oracle nuisance values** to illustrate
the interface. In an application, replace the oracle columns with aligned
predictions of the two conditional outcome means and treatment propensity.
The estimator does not fit these nuisance models.

```{r cate}
library(RdistNN)

demo <- cate_demo_data(n = 180, p = 2, design = "hetero", seed = 1)
d <- demo$data
d$m1_oracle <- d$m0_oracle + d$tau_oracle

fit_cate <- cate_dnn(
  data = d, x_cols = c("X1", "X2"),
  y_col = "Y", t_col = "D",
  m0_col = "m0_oracle", m1_col = "m1_oracle", e_col = "e_oracle",
  x0 = c(0, 0), k = 1L, se = TRUE,
  return = c("W", "dx", "psi", "nuisance")
)

summary(fit_cate)$coefficients
confint(fit_cate)
predict(fit_cate, x0 = c(0.2, -0.1), interval = "confidence")
```

The matrix interface also accepts a previously constructed pseudo-outcome:
`cate_dnn(X = X, x0 = x0, pseudo_outcome = psi)`. The
[getting-started guide](https://JakobJuergens.github.io/RdistNN/articles/getting-started.html)
shows both input formats and how to inspect local treatment overlap.

## Nonparametric regression

```{r regression}
demo_np <- np_demo_data(n = 180, p = 2, design = "sinusoidal", seed = 2)
fit_np <- np_dnn(
  data = demo_np$data, x_cols = c("X1", "X2"), y_col = "Y",
  x0 = c(0, 0), k = 1L, se = TRUE, return = c("W", "dx", "ess")
)

fit_np$mu
fit_np$se
as.data.frame(diagnostics(fit_np))[, c("target_id", "n_eff", "weighted_mean_y")]
```

For matrices, use `np_dnn(X = X, x0 = x0, Y = y)`. Regression results expose
`mu` and `se` directly and support the common diagnostics and plotting calls.
Two-scale regression uses `np_tdnn()` with explicit `s1 < s2` (`s2 < n` for
jackknife standard errors). See `?np_tdnn` for its signed weights and
additional assumptions, and `plot_tdnn_scales()` to compare component scales.

## Conditional LATE (experimental)

With a binary instrument and binary treatment, `clate_dnn()` estimates the
conditional effect among compliers under the IV assumptions. Supply the
instrument propensity and the conditional means of the outcome and treatment
in each **instrument arm**. Predictions may use more adjustment covariates
than the reporting coordinates selected by `x_cols`.

This simulated example again uses explicitly labelled oracle predictions.

```{r clate}
demo_iv <- clate_demo_data(n = 180, seed = 3, heterogeneous = TRUE)
iv <- demo_iv$data
targets <- rbind(c(.25, .25), c(.5, .5), c(.75, .75))

fit_clate <- clate_dnn(
  data = iv, x_cols = c("X1", "X2"), X0 = targets,
  y_col = "Y", d_col = "D", a_col = "A", e_col = "e_oracle",
  m_y0_col = "m_y0_oracle", m_y1_col = "m_y1_oracle",
  m_d0_col = "m_d0_oracle", m_d1_col = "m_d1_oracle",
  k = 1L, training = "oracle", return = c("W", "dx", "nuisance")
)

summary(fit_clate)$coefficients
summary(fit_clate)$components  # adjusted reduced form and first stage
```

Both component means use the same DNN weights. The ratio's uncertainty
retains their paired covariance, holding the supplied signals fixed.
`affine_ratio_dnn()` accepts the signals directly; `iv_augmented_signals()`
constructs them from predictions. The
[CLATE guide](https://JakobJuergens.github.io/RdistNN/articles/conditional-late.html)
covers input alignment, diagnostics and reporting. The
[inference guide](https://JakobJuergens.github.io/RdistNN/articles/conditional-late-inference.html)
explains denominator status and `ratio_confidence_set()`, including unbounded
sets. Inspect the first stage alongside the ratio; ordinary Wald intervals
can be misleading when the first stage is weak.

## Shared reporting and plots

CATE and CLATE use the same calls, with the fitted object's class selecting
the appropriate implementation:

```r
summary(fit)$coefficients
coef(fit)
confint(fit)
predict(fit, X0 = new_profiles, interval = "confidence")
diagnostics(fit)
```

Their coefficient tables contain `estimate`, `std.error`, `statistic`,
`p.value`, `conf.low` and `conf.high`. CLATE also reports component and
computation-status tables. Prediction changes the reporting profiles while
retaining the supplied observations and signals; it does not retrain learners.

With ggplot2 installed, use the same plotting functions for either fit:

```{r clate-plot, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, dpi = 150, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2}
plot_estimates(fit_clate, style = "forest")
```

| Call | What it shows |
|---|---|
| `plot(fit)` or `plot_estimates(fit)` | Estimates and pointwise confidence bounds; profile, forest or pointrange styles |
| `plot_weights(fit)` | Localization and weight concentration |
| `plot_overlap(fit)` | Treatment overlap for CATE; **instrument** overlap for CLATE |
| `plot_influence(fit)` | CATE score contributions or CLATE paired-score residual contributions |
| `plot_tuning(fit)` | Sensitivity across stored tuning candidates |
| `plot_dashboard(fit)` | A combined view; uses patchwork when installed, otherwise returns a named list of panels |

Retain `return = c("W", "dx", "nuisance")` for weight, distance and overlap
views. `plot_data_estimates()`, `plot_data_weights()` and
`plot_data_diagnostics()` expose data for your own plots. See the
[visualization guide](https://JakobJuergens.github.io/RdistNN/articles/visualising-fits.html)
and the CLATE guide for method-specific panels.

A CATE profile holds other covariates fixed and evaluates a sequence of
reporting targets. This example uses oracle nuisances and holds `X2` at zero.

```{r cate-profile, eval = requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE), message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, dpi = 150, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.2}
set.seed(42)
n <- 1000
X <- cbind(X1 = runif(n, -2, 2), X2 = rnorm(n))
e <- plogis(0.4 * X[, "X1"])
tau <- 1 + sin(X[, "X1"])
m0 <- X[, "X1"] - 0.5 * X[, "X2"]
treat <- as.integer(runif(n) < e)
Y <- m0 + treat * tau + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)

profile_data <- data.frame(X, T = treat, Y = Y, e = e, m0 = m0, m1 = m0 + tau)
X0 <- cbind(X1 = seq(-1.8, 1.8, length.out = 21), X2 = 0)

profile_fit <- cate_dnn(
  data = profile_data, x_cols = c("X1", "X2"), y_col = "Y", t_col = "T",
  e_col = "e", m0_col = "m0", m1_col = "m1",
  X0 = X0, k = 1L, se = TRUE, jackknife = "fast"
)
plot(profile_fit)
```

## Localization and tuning

With `k = 1` and no explicit `s`, the default is
`s = floor(0.4 * n^((p + 1)/(p + 2)))`. Here `s` is the subsample order:
increasing it concentrates weights closer to the target. Exact DNN weights
average over size-`s` subsamples, using the full rank permutation, with
support through rank `n - s + k`. The optional `neighbors` extra reports
the first `k` neighbors, rather than the full weight support.

Supply `s` directly, use `tuning = tuning_dnn_paper()`, or set
`tuning_mode = "grid"` to compare the paper-default sensitivity grid
`lambda = c(0.3, 0.4, 0.5, 0.75)`. The grid retains the default fit and
candidate results. `candidate_fit()` and `candidate_fits()` expose candidate
views for reporting, diagnostics and plots. This is sensitivity analysis;
it does not automatically select a tuning value or justify inference after
selection. See the
[tuning guide](https://JakobJuergens.github.io/RdistNN/articles/kernel-order-tuning.html).

Delete-one standard errors require `s < n`. `jackknife = "fast"` uses cached
ranks; `"loo"` provides the estimator-specific leave-one-out calculation.
Set `se = FALSE` to skip uncertainty calculations. The manuscript's DNN
derivations use exact weights and `k = 1`; larger fixed `k` values and
asymptotic weights are computational options requiring their corresponding
statistical conditions.

## Interpreting inference

Reported intervals are **pointwise**, not simultaneous confidence bands.
Neyman orthogonality controls first-order population nuisance drift; valid
full-sample nuisance reuse additionally needs learner accuracy and deletion
stability, together with design, overlap and localization-bias conditions.
Supplying oracle, out-of-fold or full-sample predictions does not itself
establish the conditions appropriate to that training procedure.

For nuisance-based CATE and CLATE scores, supplied propensities must be finite
and lie in `[0, 1]`; they are clipped to `[clip, 1 - clip]`, with
`clip = 1e-8` by default. Supplied pseudo-outcomes are used unchanged.
Clipping does not establish overlap. Weight ESS and overlap diagnostics
describe local support; they do not certify inference assumptions.

CLATE's causal interpretation additionally requires consistency, exclusion,
conditional instrument independence, monotonicity and positive local
compliance. It generally differs from population CATE. See the
[conditional Z-estimation guide](https://JakobJuergens.github.io/RdistNN/articles/conditional-z-estimation.html)
and the CLATE articles for the theoretical scope and limitations.

## Further documentation

- [Notation and conventions](https://JakobJuergens.github.io/RdistNN/articles/notation-and-conventions.html) explains arguments and returned quantities.
- [Diagnostics and reporting](https://JakobJuergens.github.io/RdistNN/articles/diagnostics-reporting.html) covers local support and uncertainty summaries.
- [Affine paper replication](https://JakobJuergens.github.io/RdistNN/articles/paper-affine-replication.html) documents the study-specific simulations, SIPP application and saved manuscript evidence. Locate the installed bundle with `system.file("paper-replication/affine", package = "RdistNN")`.
- The reference also includes **experimental PLQR** moment evaluation at supplied coefficients (without root solving), **experimental local IV-GMM**, simulation tools and extension interfaces.

If you installed the package with local vignettes, open the notation guide
with `vignette("notation-and-conventions", package = "RdistNN")`.

The package accompanies
[Orthogonal Inference for Conditional Z-Estimation without Cross-Fitting](https://jakobjuergens.com/research/#orthogonal-inference-conditional-z).
Use `citation("RdistNN")` for citation information.

## Help and contributions

Report problems or ask usage questions through the
[issue tracker](https://github.com/JakobJuergens/RdistNN/issues), including a
minimal reproducible example and `sessionInfo()`. Contributions are welcome;
[CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/JakobJuergens/RdistNN/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
links development procedures and the maintained interface and numerical
contracts. RdistNN is licensed under GPL version 3 or later.
